opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that Moravec's paradox is less of a paradox once you think about how long evolution has had to optimize different capabilities. Things like perception, motor control, navigating a cluttered physical environment, manipulating objects with your hands: these are capabilities that animals have been under intense selection pressure for over hundreds of millions of years. So the algorithms the brain runs for those tasks are probably extremely well optimized, close to some efficiency frontier given the hardware constraints.

Whereas something like abstract reasoning, mathematics, playing chess, writing code, those are really recent. In evolutionary terms, humans have been doing anything resembling formal reasoning for maybe tens of thousands of years at most, and doing things like advanced mathematics for a tiny fraction of that. So there's been very little time for evolution to refine the brain's machinery for those tasks. We're kind of repurposing general-purpose hardware that wasn't really built for it, and we're probably quite inefficient at it.

So when we build AI systems and find that it's relatively easy to beat humans at chess or competition math, but very hard to get a robot to fold laundry or clear a dinner table, that's what you'd expect. In the domains where humans are poorly optimized, the bar is low, and even fairly crude amounts of compute and fairly simple algorithms can surpass us. In the domains where evolution has spent enormous effort, the bar is very high, and you need a lot more compute, data, and algorithmic sophistication to match what a human or even a squirrel can do.

One implication I think people underappreciate is what this says about the order of automation. A lot of people intuitively expect that cognitive tasks we consider "hard," like research or high-level reasoning, will be the last to be automated. But Moravec's paradox suggests it might go the other way in some respects. The pure reasoning parts may fall relatively early, while things involving robust sensorimotor skill, common sense about the physical world, and long-horizon agency in messy environments may take much longer. And that matters a lot for forecasting economic impact, because a huge share of the economy is in the second category, not the first.

r001.rationale: The response says abstract reasoning and related skills are recent in evolutionary terms, so the brain’s machinery for them is poorly refined and likely inefficient.

r002.rationale: It mentions AI beating humans at chess, but does not discuss compute scaling from amateur to world-champion strength or infer a span of more than five orders of magnitude in human chess efficiency.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare variation in human chess-playing efficiency with variation in human running speed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about Moravec's paradox is basically through an evolutionary lens. The observation is that things humans find hard, like playing chess or doing symbolic mathematics or arithmetic, turned out to be relatively easy to get computers to do. And things that humans find trivially easy, like walking around a room, picking up an object, recognizing a face, turned out to be very hard. And I think the natural explanation is that the capabilities humans find easy are the ones that evolution has spent an enormous amount of time optimizing. Sensorimotor control, vision, navigating a physical environment, these are things that go back hundreds of millions of years. There's been a huge amount of selection pressure on them, and the brain has dedicated a lot of hardware to them. So when something feels effortless to us, that's not because the problem is simple. It's because we have very heavily optimized machinery for it, and the difficulty is hidden from our introspection.

Whereas things like chess or formal reasoning are evolutionarily very recent. There hasn't been time for evolution to optimize us for them, so we're running them on general-purpose machinery that wasn't really built for the task. That's why they feel hard, and that's also why there's a lot of slack. A fairly small amount of compute can beat us, because we're not very good at them in absolute terms. Human performance at chess is close to the floor of what's possible, while human performance at, say, visual object recognition or dexterous manipulation is much closer to some kind of efficient frontier given the compute involved.

And I think this has implications for how we should expect AI progress to go. The capabilities that are last to fall are plausibly the ones where humans are most optimized, which means robotics and fine motor control and real-world interaction. And the things that fall early are the ones where we have essentially no evolutionary head start. I'd also add that this makes the impressiveness of current systems a bit misleading in both directions. Something like a language model doing competition math looks very impressive to us because that's hard for humans. But in some sense that's the low-hanging fruit. The genuinely hard milestone from this perspective is something like a robot that can do what a two-year-old does with its hands, because that's where we're competing against a few hundred million years of optimization.

r001.rationale: It says evolution has spent enormous time optimizing sensorimotor abilities, while chess and formal reasoning are recent and run on general-purpose machinery not optimized for them.

r002.rationale: It says relatively little compute can beat humans at chess, but gives no scaling from average amateur to world champion and does not state a human-efficiency range spanning more than five orders of magnitude.

r003.rationale: It does not compare variation in human chess-playing efficiency with variation in running speed.

astra-6.text:
I think one way to understand Moravec’s paradox is that the things we find difficult aren’t necessarily the things that are difficult to build. How much effort something takes us is partly a reflection of how well optimized we are for doing it.

We’ve had a very long evolutionary history of interacting with the physical world: perceiving our surroundings, moving around, manipulating objects. So we have very sophisticated machinery for those things, but most of it operates without conscious effort. That makes them feel easy, even though there’s a lot of computation going on underneath.

By contrast, something like doing arithmetic or proving a theorem is much more recent. We haven’t been optimized for those tasks in the same way. We’re using capabilities that evolved for other purposes, and we find it slow and effortful. But that doesn’t mean a machine needs especially elaborate machinery to outperform us at arithmetic.

So the distinction I’d make is between how difficult a task feels to a human and how difficult it is to achieve a given level of performance on that task. If humans are already very well optimized for something, matching us could be quite hard, even if we do it effortlessly. Where we’re poorly optimized, there may be relatively simple approaches that do much better than we do.

r001.rationale: The response says effortful tasks such as arithmetic are more recent and humans have not been optimized for them in the same way.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss chess, compute scaling, or an efficiency range exceeding five orders of magnitude.

r003.rationale: It does not compare variation in chess-playing efficiency with variation in human running speed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one way to understand Moravec’s paradox is that the things we find difficult aren’t necessarily the things that are computationally difficult. They might just be things that humans aren’t particularly well optimized to do.

We’ve had a very long evolutionary history of interacting with the physical world—perceiving our surroundings, moving around, manipulating objects. So we’re extremely well optimized for those tasks, and they feel effortless to us. But something like doing arithmetic or playing chess is much more recent, and evolution hasn’t specifically optimized us for it. We have to use fairly general cognitive abilities, often quite inefficiently.

So when a computer does arithmetic much faster than we can, that doesn’t mean it has surpassed the computational sophistication involved in human perception or motor control. It may just be doing a relatively simple task with an architecture that’s much better suited to it. The difficulty we experience is a measure of the task relative to our own capabilities, rather than an absolute measure of how hard it is.
